title: Personal Finance and Investing
description: Judge which money choice costs more, and roughly how much, under Australian rules: tax, saving, borrowing, HECS-HELP, home loans, super, investing, insurance and scams.
audience: Adults and older students in Australia who earn or will earn income, and who want to judge offers and products themselves. They need percentages and nothing else. The course does not repeat the market theory in Economics or the expected value and utility in Decision Theory.
outcomes: You'll be able to read an ATO tax table for a stated year and say how much of an extra dollar you keep.
You'll be able to size an emergency fund in months of spending and decide where to hold it.
You'll be able to judge, from rate, time and fees, which of two credit, loan or fund choices costs more and roughly by how much.
You'll be able to tell the true cost of an 'interest-free' or buy now pay later offer from its conditions.
You'll be able to explain how super contributions, caps, fees and access work, and test a contribution against the cap.
You'll be able to match an investment mix to a goal's time frame and say what diversification does and does not remove.
You'll be able to match insurance to risks and spot the pressure and payment patterns of a scam.

lessons.title: From gross pay to take-home
lessons.objective: Read an Australian income tax table for a stated year and say how much of an extra dollar of pay is kept, why that differs from the average rate, and what the 2% Medicare levy adds.

concepts.title: Tax band
concepts.summary: Each rate applies only to the income that falls inside its band, as in '30c for each $1 over $45,000'.

concepts.title: Marginal rate
concepts.summary: The rate on the next dollar earned. It decides how much of a raise or an extra shift is kept.

concepts.title: Average rate
concepts.summary: Total tax divided by taxable income. It is lower than the marginal rate once income passes the first bands.

concepts.title: Medicare levy
concepts.summary: 2% of taxable income, charged on top of the table. The ATO's rates do not include it.

concepts.title: Income year
concepts.summary: Rates belong to a stated financial year: the first band was 16c in 2025-26 and is 15c in 2026-27.

misconceptions: Crossing a band taxes the whole income at the higher rate, so a raise can leave you worse off. The table says 'for each $1 over', so only the dollars above the line move up.
The average rate is the rate on the next dollar. At $135,000 the tax is $31,020, about 23%, but the next dollar is taxed at 37c.
The table already includes the Medicare levy. The ATO notes under each year that it does not.
Tax rates are fixed. 2025-26 and 2026-27 differ in the first two bands, so a figure with no year attached cannot be trusted.
sequence: Open on the 2026-27 table (ato-tax) and read what '15c for each $1 over $18,200' says about the first dollars.
Take a worker at $44,000 offered $46,000. Only $1,000 of the raise sits above $45,000; the raise adds about $450 of tax, not $600 and not a whole-income re-tax.
Average against marginal at $100,000: tax $20,520 (20.5%), next dollar 30c.
Add the 2% levy: a $10,000 raise at $100,000 keeps about $6,800.
Put the 2025-26 table beside it: the same $40,000 income pays about $3,488 in 2025-26 and $3,270 in 2026-27 (derived). A budget built on last year's table is off by hundreds.
Say what the table leaves out (offsets, surcharges, HELP, deductions) without teaching them.

figures.learnerAction: Choose an income and read which band its last dollar is in.

questionPlan.sample: Priya's taxable income is $44,000 in 2026-27 and she is offered a raise to $46,000. Using the ATO table (shown), what happens to her tax?
choices: Only the $1,000 above $45,000 is taxed at 30c; the rest of her income stays in the 15c band
All $46,000 is now taxed at 30c, so she takes home less than before
Her tax rises by $600, because the whole $2,000 raise is taxed at 30c
Her tax does not change until her income passes $135,000
questionPlan.answer: Only the $1,000 above $45,000 is taxed at 30c; the rest of her income stays in the 15c band

wrongBecause.All $46,000 is now taxed at 30c, so she: Treats a band as a cliff: the 30c applies only to dollars above $45,000.
wrongBecause.Her tax rises by $600, because the whole: Forgets that the first $1,000 of the raise is still inside the 15c band.
wrongBecause.Her tax does not change until her income: Confuses the next band's start with the top rate band.

questionPlan.sample: Dev's taxable income is $100,000 in 2026-27 and he gets a $10,000 raise. Using the table and the 2% levy, roughly how much of the raise does he keep, in dollars?
questionPlan.accepts: 6500 to 7100; $7,950 shows the average rate was used, $7,000 shows the levy was left out

questionPlan.sample: Mia's taxable income is exactly $135,000, and her tax is $31,020, about 23% of it. She is offered $100 of overtime pay. About how much does she keep after income tax and the Medicare levy?
choices: About $61
About $77
About $63
About $70
questionPlan.answer: About $61

wrongBecause.About $77: Uses her 23% average rate instead of the rate on the next dollar.
wrongBecause.About $63: Takes off the 37c band and forgets the 2c Medicare levy.
wrongBecause.About $70: Uses the 30c band, but her next dollar is in the 37c band.

questionPlan.sample: A budgeting spreadsheet taxes income from $18,201 to $45,000 at 16c and calls its 2026-27 take-home figures exact. What is the most likely problem?
choices: It uses the 2025-26 rate; the ATO's 2026-27 rate for that band is 15c
It has left out the Medicare levy, which the ATO table already includes
It is wrong in every year, because 16c was never an ATO rate
It is fine, because the ATO changes this rate only once a decade
questionPlan.answer: It uses the 2025-26 rate; the ATO's 2026-27 rate for that band is 15c

wrongBecause.It has left out the Medicare levy, which: The table does not include the levy; and the leftover rate is the clearer fault.
wrongBecause.It is wrong in every year, because 16c w: 16c was the rate in 2025-26, so the figure is right for an earlier year.
wrongBecause.It is fine, because the ATO changes this: The first two bands changed between 2025-26 and 2026-27.

lessons.title: Budgets and emergency funds
lessons.objective: Sort a month of household spending into essentials, debt repayments and irregular costs, say whether it leaves a surplus, and size and place an emergency fund in months of spending.

concepts.title: Budget
concepts.summary: A list of the money coming in and the money going out, checked against bank statements and reviewed monthly.

concepts.title: Irregular costs
concepts.summary: Annual bills and surprises such as car registration or a vet bill. They break a budget that lists only monthly bills.

concepts.title: Surplus
concepts.summary: What is left when expenses are taken from income. It is where saving comes from.

concepts.title: Emergency fund
concepts.summary: Money kept for urgent, unexpected costs. A good target is three months of expenses.

concepts.title: Where to keep it
concepts.summary: A separate account, or an offset account on a home loan, so that it is easy to reach and hard to spend by accident.

misconceptions: A budget lists regular bills only. The annual and unexpected costs are the ones that push people onto a credit card.
An emergency fund is a dollar target. It is a number of months of spending, so $9,000 can be three months for one household and two for another.
A sale, a holiday deal or an investment opportunity is an emergency. The fund is for expenses that must be paid quickly when other money is not available.
An offset account earns interest for you. It reduces the loan balance that interest is charged on while the money stays reachable.
sequence: A month of invented household figures (labelled invented): income, then expenses in three groups (moneysmart).
Irregular costs: turn an annual bill into a monthly share and see how a month looks different.
Compare income and expenses: surplus or shortfall, and which lines can move.
Set the goal in months of spending (three is the pack's target); $20 a week is over $1,000 in a year.
Where to hold it: a separate account, or an offset account if there is a home loan. What counts as an emergency, using the page's own example of a car breakdown.
examples: Invented: Household A holds $9,000 and spends $3,000 a month (3 months of cover); Household B holds $9,000 and spends $4,500 (2 months).
Moneysmart's Eva saves $10 a payday, has over $1,070 after two years and spends $1,000 on a car repair without borrowing. Restate, do not quote.

figures.learnerAction: Drop each line into its group.

figures.shows: Two bars of the same $9,000 marked off in months of spending for two households.
figures.learnerAction: Read months of cover from each bar.

questionPlan.sample: These are lines from an invented household budget. Which group does each belong to?
items: Car registration, paid once a year
Vet bill after a dog's accident
questionPlan.answer: Essential: Rent, Electricity bill; Debt repayment: Personal loan repayment, Credit card payment; Irregular or unexpected: Car registration, paid once a year, Vet bill after a dog's accident

questionPlan.sample: Two households each hold $9,000 in savings. Household A spends $3,000 a month and household B spends $4,500 a month. Which has the bigger safety net?
choices: Household A: its savings cover three months and B's cover two
They are the same, because both hold $9,000
Household B, because it has more spending to protect
Household B, because a larger spender needs a smaller fund
questionPlan.answer: Household A: its savings cover three months and B's cover two

wrongBecause.They are the same, because both hold $9,: Measures the fund in dollars, not in months of spending.
wrongBecause.Household B, because it has more spendin: Mixes up the size of the need with the size of the cover.
wrongBecause.Household B, because a larger spender ne: Reverses the reasoning: more spending needs more savings for the same cover.

questionPlan.sample: Which of these is a job for an emergency fund?
choices: The family car's gearbox fails and the car is needed to get to work this week
A holiday booked at 40% off must be paid for by tomorrow
Council rates are due in March, as in every year
A deposit for a first home
questionPlan.answer: The family car's gearbox fails and the car is needed to get to work this week

wrongBecause.A holiday booked at 40% off must be paid: A bargain is an opportunity, not an urgent cost; it can wait or be saved for.
wrongBecause.Council rates are due in March, as in ev: A known annual bill belongs in the budget as an irregular cost.
wrongBecause.A deposit for a first home: A savings goal, not an unexpected cost.

questionPlan.sample: Priya has a home loan with an offset account and $12,000 of emergency savings. What does keeping the $12,000 in the offset do that a separate savings account does not?
choices: It cuts the loan balance interest is charged on while she can still reach the money
It pays her interest, so the fund grows faster than the loan
It locks the money until the loan is paid off, which stops her spending it
It makes the savings part of the home loan, so she can no longer withdraw them
questionPlan.answer: It cuts the loan balance interest is charged on while she can still reach the money

wrongBecause.It pays her interest, so the fund grows: An offset saves loan interest; it does not pay interest to her.
wrongBecause.It locks the money until the loan is pai: An offset works like an everyday account; the money stays reachable.
wrongBecause.It makes the savings part of the home lo: That describes extra repayments into the loan, which may or may not be redrawable.

lessons.title: Compounding, inflation and time
lessons.objective: Judge from a rate, a time and a starting amount how fast a balance grows, use the Rule of 72 to estimate doubling, and say when a rate fails to keep up with prices.

concepts.title: Compound interest
concepts.summary: Interest earned on the principal and on interest already added.

concepts.title: Simple interest
concepts.summary: Interest on the starting amount only.

concepts.title: Rule of 72
concepts.summary: Years to double is roughly 72 divided by the yearly rate in per cent.

concepts.title: Inflation and CPI
concepts.summary: The rate at which the prices of what households buy rise; the CPI measures it on a basket of goods and services.

concepts.title: Keeping up with prices
concepts.summary: A rate below the inflation rate leaves a balance that buys less; HELP indexation keeps a debt in line with prices.

misconceptions: Interest earns the same dollars every year. At the same 3% the pack's account earns $1,616 in its first five years and $1,878 in the next five.
Doubling takes 100 divided by the rate in years. That is the simple-interest answer (about 17 years at 6%); compounding gives about 12.
A positive rate always makes you better off. If prices rise faster than the balance, it buys less.
How often interest is added matters more than rate or time. In the pack it is worth $334 on $10,000 over 5 years, while 20 years earns $8,208 at 3%.
sequence: Read Moneysmart's figures for $10,000 at 3% compounded monthly: $11,616, $13,494, $18,208 at 5, 10 and 20 years.
Interest on interest: the interest earned in years 6 to 10 ($1,878) against years 1 to 5 ($1,616) at the same rate.
Simple against compound: Lorenzo and Sophia (5%, 5 years): $12,500 against $12,834.
The Rule of 72: use it to estimate doubling at 3%, 6% and 9%; check it against Moneysmart's balances.
Inflation: define it with the RBA's wording; a 3% account when prices rise 4% (made-up); HELP indexation as the same idea in a debt.
examples: Rule of 72 against exact doubling (derived): 6% gives 12 years by the rule and 11.9 exactly; 3% gives 24 and 23.4; 9% gives 8 and 8.04.
Invented: account at 3%, prices rising 4%: the balance is 3% bigger but each dollar buys about 1% less.

figures.shows: Balance over 20 years for compound and simple interest at the same rate, as two lines.
figures.learnerAction: Change the rate and the number of years and read the gap.

figures.shows: Interest earned in each five-year block from the pack's $10,000 at 3% example: 1,616; 1,878; and the 11-20 year total.
figures.learnerAction: Read why the later blocks are taller.

questionPlan.sample: $10,000 at 3% compounded monthly earns $1,616 in its first five years and a further $1,878 in the next five. Why is the second figure larger when the rate has not changed?
choices: Later interest is worked out on a bigger balance that includes interest already added
The bank raises the rate once the account is five years old
Interest is added more often in the later years
Money earns more simply because it has been held for longer, whatever the balance
questionPlan.answer: Later interest is worked out on a bigger balance that includes interest already added

wrongBecause.The bank raises the rate once the accoun: The rate in the example is fixed at 3%.
wrongBecause.Interest is added more often in the late: The compounding frequency (monthly) does not change.
wrongBecause.Money earns more simply because it has b: Interest is calculated on the balance; time matters only because the balance grows.

questionPlan.sample: About how many years does money take to double at 6% a year with interest compounding? Give the nearest whole number of years.
questionPlan.accepts: 11 to 13; 17 shows 100 divided by the rate (the simple-interest instinct)

questionPlan.sample: An account pays 3% a year while prices are rising 4% a year (made-up figures). After one year, which is true?
choices: The balance is 3% bigger but buys less than before
The balance buys the same as before, because interest covers the price rise
The balance buys 3% more than before
The balance buys 4% more than before
questionPlan.answer: The balance is 3% bigger but buys less than before

wrongBecause.The balance buys the same as before, bec: Interest of 3% does not cover a 4% rise.
wrongBecause.The balance buys 4% more than before: Counts the price rise as a gain.

questionPlan.sample: Lorenzo and Sophia each put $10,000 in at 5% for 5 years. Sophia ends with $12,834 and Lorenzo with $12,500. What explains the $334?
choices: Sophia's interest is added monthly and then earns interest; Lorenzo's arrives only at the end
Sophia was paid a higher rate than Lorenzo
Sophia paid in more money than Lorenzo
Monthly interest is a larger rate than yearly interest
questionPlan.answer: Sophia's interest is added monthly and then earns interest; Lorenzo's arrives only at the end

wrongBecause.Monthly interest is a larger rate than y: The yearly rate is the same; the monthly additions then earn interest of their own.

lessons.title: Credit cards
lessons.objective: Say what a credit card costs for a given pattern of use, choose between two cards for someone who pays in full and someone who carries a balance, and judge whether a rewards program is worth its fee.

concepts.title: Purchase rate
concepts.summary: The yearly interest rate on purchases once any interest-free period has not applied. The average is over 18%.

concepts.title: Interest-free days
concepts.summary: Days with no interest on purchases, which apply only if the full balance is paid by the due date.

concepts.title: Card fees
concepts.summary: Annual or monthly fee, rewards program fee, late fee, cash advance fee, overseas fee.

concepts.title: Credit risk
concepts.summary: The bank's view of the chance of not being repaid, which the RBA says lifts card rates above home-loan rates.

concepts.title: Balance transfer
concepts.summary: Moving a debt to a card or loan with a low or 0% introductory rate; it saves money only if repaid in that period.

misconceptions: Interest-free days apply to every purchase on every card. They apply only when the whole balance is paid by the due date.
The card with the lowest annual fee is the cheapest. For someone who carries a balance the rate dominates; for someone who pays in full the fee and the days matter.
The minimum repayment is the sensible amount to pay. Paying more than the minimum clears the debt sooner and cuts the interest.
Rewards are a free extra. In Moneysmart's example $5,700 of spending earns a $25 gift card and the program costs $30 a year.
sequence: Start with the scale (RBA figures quoted by Moneysmart): about 14.7 million cards, about $33 billion owed, almost $18 billion accruing interest, average rate over 18%.
Why the rate is that high: the RBA's account of credit risk against home loans.
Two uses, two best cards: full payers want interest-free days; carriers want a low rate and low fee.
Rewards as a judgement: points earned per dollar against the fee.
Paying down several cards: minimums on all, extra on the highest rate (cheapest) or the smallest balance (motivation).
examples: Invented cards, labelled so: Card A has 55 interest-free days, a $120 annual fee and a 21% purchase rate; Card B has no frills, a $59 annual fee and a 13% rate.
Jen's rewards (restate): $30 a year, $5,700 of spending for a $25 gift card, about 0.4c back per dollar.

figures.shows: Two invented cards side by side: interest-free days, annual fee, purchase rate, rewards fee.
figures.learnerAction: Read which features matter to a named user.

figures.shows: A statement period as a timeline with the due date, showing interest-free days applying only on the line where the balance is paid in full.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between paid in full and part paid.

questionPlan.sample: Card A (invented) has 55 interest-free days, a $120 annual fee and a 21% rate. Card B has a $59 fee and a 13% rate. Which card suits each person?
items: Mia pays the full balance every month
Tom usually carries about $4,000 from month to month
Ana pays in full and often uses the whole interest-free period
Ravi keeps a $2,500 balance on the card all year
questionPlan.answer: Card A: Mia pays the full balance every month, Ana pays in full and often uses the whole interest-free period; Card B: Tom usually carries about $4,000 from month to month, Ravi keeps a $2,500 balance on the card all year

questionPlan.sample: Jen is offered a rewards program that costs $30 a year to join. She would have to spend $5,700 to earn a $25 gift card. What does that show?
choices: At that spending the reward ($25) is worth less than the fee ($30), and it returns under half a cent per dollar spent
The reward is free money, because the points never cost anything to earn
The program is worth joining, because $30 is a small fee
The fee is the cost of the card, so the rewards are extra and cannot lose her money
questionPlan.answer: At that spending the reward ($25) is worth less than the fee ($30), and it returns under half a cent per dollar spent

wrongBecause.The reward is free money, because the po: Points are paid for with the fee and with the spending.
wrongBecause.The program is worth joining, because $3: A fee is small only against what it buys; here it exceeds the reward.
wrongBecause.The fee is the cost of the card, so the: The fee is charged for the rewards program and can exceed the reward.

questionPlan.sample: A bank charges 6.25% on a home loan and 19% on a credit card. According to the RBA, what best explains the gap?
choices: The bank judges it more likely to lose money on card loans than on home loans and sets the rate to match
Money lent on cards costs the bank three times as much to borrow
The RBA sets card rates separately from home loan rates
Card rates are set by the card network and not by the bank
questionPlan.answer: The bank judges it more likely to lose money on card loans than on home loans and sets the rate to match

wrongBecause.Money lent on cards costs the bank three: Funding costs are one input; the RBA names the chance of non-repayment as the reason for the gap.
wrongBecause.The RBA sets card rates separately from: The RBA sets the cash rate; banks set their own lending rates.
wrongBecause.Card rates are set by the card network a: The bank sets the lending rate.

questionPlan.sample: Hana owes $900 on Card A at 14%, $3,000 on Card B at 27% and $6,000 on Card C at 21% (made-up). She can pay $300 a month above the minimums. Which card gets the extra to cut her interest bill most?
choices: Card B, the highest rate
Card A, the smallest balance
Card C, the biggest balance
All three equally, to be fair
questionPlan.answer: Card B, the highest rate

wrongBecause.Card A, the smallest balance: Clearing the smallest balance gives quick progress, which helps motivation, but it saves less interest.
wrongBecause.Card C, the biggest balance: The size of the debt matters less than the rate charged on it.
wrongBecause.All three equally, to be fair: Spreading the extra gives up the larger saving on the dearest debt.

lessons.title: Interest-free offers and buy now pay later
lessons.objective: Work out what an interest-free or buy now pay later offer will cost under its conditions, and find the condition that turns 'free' into a debt.

concepts.title: Buy now pay later
concepts.summary: Paying by instalments, usually without interest and with fees instead.

concepts.title: BNPL fees
concepts.summary: Late fees, monthly account-keeping fees, payment processing fees and establishment fees; bank overdrawn fees can follow.

concepts.title: Interest-free deal
concepts.summary: A period (such as 12, 24 or 60 months) with no interest on the purchase, usually through a store card or credit card. The retailer is not the lender.

concepts.title: The minimum-repayment trap
concepts.summary: Minimum repayments will not clear the balance by the end date, and interest, up to 29%, can then be charged on what is left.

concepts.title: Credit file effects
concepts.summary: Applications trigger credit checks and late or missed payments can be reported.

misconceptions: Interest-free means cost-free. Fees may apply, and interest can be charged on any balance left at the end.
Paying the minimum repayments clears an interest-free deal by its end date. Moneysmart says it will not.
BNPL leaves no record. Each application is a credit check and late payments can be reported.
Several BNPL services spread the risk. They make it harder to keep track, as Georgia found when her account was overdrawn.
The store is the lender. Check the contract: it is not.
sequence: Read the headline, then the conditions: which card, which fees, what happens at the end.
BNPL fees: which come from the service and which from the bank.
Three styles of interest-free deal: equal instalments, minimum repayment, deferred payment.
The minimum-repayment trap with numbers (invented): a $3,000 deal over 24 months with a $60 minimum leaves $1,560.
July 2026: the Federal Court penalties for a 60-month interest-free advertisement (restate from moneysmart; the pack has no court source).
Alternatives: lay-by, a No Interest Loan, saving up.
examples: Invented: $3,000 couch, 24 months interest-free, $60 minimum a month: $60 x 24 = $1,440 repaid, $1,560 left. Splitting $3,000 into 24 equal payments gives $125 a month.
Moneysmart's Georgia: sneakers $150 on one BNPL service, a $300 straightener on another; account overdrawn a fortnight later.

figures.shows: Two invented offers with their headline and their fine print: eligible card, fees, what happens at the end.
figures.learnerAction: Find the line that changes the cost.

figures.shows: A 24-month timeline for an invented $2,400 deal paying the minimum against equal instalments, with the balance at the end date.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between the two payment styles.

questionPlan.sample: A $3,000 couch is on a 24-month interest-free deal (made-up). The minimum repayment is $60 a month and the buyer pays only the minimum for 24 months. What happens at the end?
choices: About $1,560 is still owed, and interest can now be charged on it
Nothing is owed, because an interest-free deal is repaid by its minimum payments
About $1,560 is owed, but it stays interest-free until it is paid
The retailer writes off what is left
questionPlan.answer: About $1,560 is still owed, and interest can now be charged on it

wrongBecause.Nothing is owed, because an interest-fre: Minimum repayments will not pay off the total by the end of the period.
wrongBecause.About $1,560 is owed, but it stays inter: Interest-free applies to the promotional period; interest can be charged on the balance after it.
wrongBecause.The retailer writes off what is left: The retailer is not the lender, and the debt remains.

questionPlan.sample: Which of these does a buy now pay later service itself charge?
bins: Not charged by the BNPL service
items: Not charged by the BNPL service
An overdrawn fee when the bank account lacks the money
Not charged by the BNPL service
questionPlan.answer: Charged by the BNPL service: A late payment fee, A monthly account-keeping fee, An establishment fee; Not charged by the BNPL service: Interest on the purchase amount, An overdrawn fee when the bank account lacks the money

questionPlan.sample: Georgia buys $150 sneakers with one BNPL service and a $300 straightener with another. A fortnight later her bank account is overdrawn. What went wrong?
choices: Two services each took a repayment from the same account and she had not checked she could cover both
The first service charged interest that she was not told about
BNPL only allows one service at a time, so the second purchase broke the rules
The overdrawn fee is a BNPL late fee

wrongBecause.The first service charged interest that: BNPL usually charges fees, not interest, and nothing says interest was charged.
wrongBecause.BNPL only allows one service at a time,: Several services can be used at once; that is the problem.
wrongBecause.The overdrawn fee is a BNPL late fee: An overdrawn fee is charged by the bank.

questionPlan.sample: In July 2026 the Federal Court imposed $35 million (Harvey Norman) and $20 million (Latitude Finance) in penalties over an advertisement for a 60-month interest-free deal (as reported by Moneysmart). What did the Court find the advertisement did not adequately disclose?
choices: That buyers had to use a specified credit card and pay the applicable fees
That the deal was shorter than 60 months
That the goods cost more at Harvey Norman than elsewhere
That interest-free deals can only be used once a year

lessons.title: HECS-HELP
lessons.objective: Read a HELP repayment table and an indexation table to say what the debt grows by, what repaying takes from pay at a given income, and how a voluntary repayment compares with other debts.

concepts.title: HELP debt
concepts.summary: A study loan repaid through the tax system. It is not charged interest but is indexed.

concepts.title: Repayment income
concepts.summary: Taxable income plus reportable fringe benefits, net investment losses, reportable super contributions and exempt foreign income.

concepts.title: Marginal repayment
concepts.summary: From 2025-26 the compulsory repayment is worked out only on the income above each threshold (2026-27: nil to $69,528, then 15c per $1, then 17c per $1 above $129,717).

concepts.title: Indexation
concepts.summary: Applied on 1 June to the part of the debt older than 11 months, at the lower of CPI and WPI growth. Like interest, it makes the debt grow.

concepts.title: Voluntary repayment
concepts.summary: A repayment made before 1 June (at least 5 business days) accrues less indexation.

misconceptions: HELP is interest-bearing like a bank loan. It is indexed, not charged interest, though the debt grows like it does (2.8% in 2026).
Once over the threshold, repayment is a flat share of all income. From 2025-26 each rate applies only to the income above its threshold.
If nothing is paid the debt stays the same. Indexation raises it each 1 June.

Repayment income is taxable income. It adds fringe benefits, investment losses and reportable super contributions.

concepts.title: Principal and interest

concepts.title: Loan term

concepts.title: Key Facts Sheet

concepts.title: Offset account

lessons.title: How super works
lessons.objective: Say who pays into super, how each kind of contribution is taxed and capped, and when the money can be taken out, then judge a contribution or an early-access offer.

concepts.title: Super guarantee
concepts.summary: The minimum employer contribution: 12% from 1 July 2025, paid on top of wages; from 1 July 2026 it is worked out on qualifying earnings.

concepts.title: Concessional contributions
concepts.summary: Before-tax contributions: employer contributions, salary sacrifice, and personal contributions claimed as a deduction. Capped at $32,500 in 2026-27 across all funds, and taxed at 15% in the fund.

concepts.title: Non-concessional contributions
concepts.summary: After-tax contributions, capped at $130,000 in 2026-27.

concepts.title: Preservation and conditions of release
concepts.summary: Super is preserved until a condition is met: turning 65, or reaching preservation age (55 to 60 by birth date; 60 from 1 July 1964) and retiring.

concepts.title: Illegal early access
concepts.summary: Schemes that release super for credit card debt, a car or a holiday are illegal; the amount is taxed as income and penalties apply.

misconceptions: Super is taken out of your wages. It is paid on top of them.
The cap counts only what you add. It counts employer contributions too, across all your funds.
The guarantee has always been 12%. It was 9% from 2002 to 2013 and rose in steps to 12% in 2025-26.
A firm that sets up a self-managed fund can legally release your super for a debt or a holiday. It is illegal and the amount is taxed as income.
Salary sacrifice saves the same tax for everyone. The gain is the gap between your marginal rate and the 15% charged in the fund.
sequence: The guarantee table (ato-super): 9% to 12% across the years; what the base is (ordinary time earnings, then qualifying earnings from 1 July 2026; overtime generally not included).
Paid on top of wages, not out of them (Wikipedia); who the fund is for.
Concessional and non-concessional: which is which, and which is taxed at 15%.
Caps for 2026-27, with Ana's numbers: employer SG counts, so $14,400 plus $20,000 exceeds $32,500.
15% against a marginal rate: Lin at 17% (15c plus levy) gains little, Omar at 32% gains about $170 per $1,000 (derived).

concepts.summary: Shares, fixed income including bonds, property and cash.

concepts.title: Index fund

questionPlan.answer: Spreading across many companies helps: One company's shares collapse after a fraud, A mine floods and one mining company falls; Spreading across many companies does not help: The whole Australian share market falls 20%, Rising interest rates push down the value of shares generally

questionPlan.sample: Kyle holds shares in five mining companies. Is he diversified?
choices: No: five companies in one sector share the risk of a fall in commodity prices
Yes: five holdings are enough to diversify
Yes: the companies have different names and mines
No: he would need at least 30 shares to be diversified in any case

lessons.title: Property against shares
lessons.objective: Compare an investment property with a share fund on cash flow, costs, concentration and borrowing, and say what a property would have to do to cover a monthly shortfall.

concepts.title: Cash-flow shortfall
concepts.summary: Rent less loan repayments and costs. Simon and Tiana's is $1,416 a month.

concepts.title: Entry, exit and ongoing costs
concepts.summary: Stamp duty, legal and agent's fees at purchase and sale; body corporate, management and repairs while owning.

concepts.title: Gearing
concepts.summary: Borrowing to invest, which magnifies both gains and losses, and the loan must be repaid whatever the investment does.

concepts.title: Margin call
concepts.summary: A demand to cut a loan back when its ratio to the investment's value passes the lender's limit (usually 70%).

concepts.title: Concentration
concepts.summary: One asset in one place carries the risk of that place.

misconceptions: Property is the safe, simple option. The pack says it can seem so but has pitfalls.
The rent pays the loan. Simon and Tiana's rent covers $2,250 of $3,666 of monthly costs.
A 20% fall loses 20% of what you put in. With borrowing, Kyle's 20% fall cost half of his own $10,000.
Costs arise only at purchase. Entry and exit costs are large and ownership has its own.
Tax makes the shortfall disappear. The 2026 Budget changed negative gearing and CGT, and the pack does not say how.
sequence: Read Simon and Tiana's table: price $550,000, buying costs $23,000, deposit $150,000, borrowing $423,000; monthly shortfall $1,416.
What must happen to cover it: about $17,000 a year, or about 3% of the price (derived), before selling costs.
Costs on entry and exit, and while owning; vacancy.
Concentration: one property in one place; a fund of many holdings.
Kyle's margin call: LVR 60%, a $5,000 fall, 75% against a 70% limit.
What the pack does not say: the Budget's tax changes.
examples: Derived: costs total $2,725 + $225 + $216 + $500 = $3,666; rent covers 61%.
Kyle: own $10,000 + $15,000 borrowed = $25,000; a $5,000 fall is 20% of the shares and 50% of his own money.

lessons.title: Insurance
lessons.objective: Match income protection, life, TPD and health cover to the risk each one covers, read the features that decide what a policy pays, and judge whether a hospital policy or the Medicare levy surcharge costs more.

concepts.title: Income protection
concepts.summary: Replaces a percentage of pre-tax income (for example 75% or 90%) when illness or injury stops work; the waiting period (14 days to two years) and the benefit period (two or five years, or to a set age) decide how much is paid.

concepts.title: Life cover
concepts.summary: A lump sum on death, which matters when others depend on your income or you carry large debts; the amount is what is needed minus what would be received.

concepts.title: Insurance through super
concepts.summary: Default cover is paid for out of the balance, which reduces retirement savings.

concepts.title: Health cover
concepts.summary: Ambulance, hospital and extras. Premiums are community rated and waiting periods apply.

concepts.title: Medicare levy surcharge
concepts.summary: 0%, 1%, 1.25% or 1.5% of income for MLS purposes, on the whole income, for those over the threshold without an appropriate level of hospital cover.

misconceptions: Everyone needs life cover. If no one depends on your income you may not, and income protection may fit better.
Income protection pays the whole income. It pays a percentage of pre-tax income after a wait, for a limited benefit period.
The surcharge applies only to income above the threshold. It applies to the whole income: $1,050 at $105,001 for a single person without hospital cover in 2026-27.
Extras cover satisfies the surcharge. Hospital cover does; extras alone does not.
Default cover in super is free. Premiums come out of the balance.
sequence: Begin from the risks, not the products: unable to work, dying with dependants, needing hospital care.
Income protection features on a timeline: waiting period, then benefit period.
Life cover: the gap between what is needed and what would be received.
Cover inside and outside super.
Health cover: ambulance, hospital, extras; community rating and waiting periods.
The surcharge table and Tom's example; the lifetime loading (2% a year, so first cover at 40 means 20%).
Compare surcharge and premium at two incomes.
examples: ATO 2026-27: single tiers $105,000, $123,000, $164,000 at 0%, 1%, 1.25%, 1.5%. Tom: income for MLS purposes $117,000, surcharge $1,170.
Derived: at $105,001 the surcharge is 1% of the whole, about $1,050; at $125,000 it is 1.25%, about $1,562.
Invented, labelled: Rav has a 30 day waiting period and a two year benefit period, and cannot work for three years.

choices: At $117,000 the surcharge costs less than the premium, but at $125,000 it would be about $1,562, more than the policy, which also pays hospital costs
Always buy the policy, because the surcharge is a penalty
Never buy the policy, because the surcharge is cheaper
The surcharge applies only to the part of his income above $123,000

wrongBecause.The surcharge applies only to the part o: It applies to the whole income at the tier rate.

lessons.title: Scams
lessons.objective: Recognise the pressure, payment and trust-building patterns of investment and super scams in a message or advertisement, and read loss data to judge where the real losses are.

concepts.title: Investment scam
concepts.summary: A fake product offered by someone who is not who they claim to be; the product does not exist.

concepts.title: Red flags
concepts.summary: Guaranteed or very high returns, pressure to decide, no AFS licence, unregistered prospectus, payment by gift card or cryptocurrency.

concepts.title: Trust-building
concepts.summary: Scripted calls, fake platforms and small early 'profits' that make a larger payment feel safe.

concepts.title: Reports against losses
concepts.summary: The most-reported contact method is not necessarily the costliest; the median and total loss differ by method.

concepts.title: Stop, Check, Protect
concepts.summary: Do not pay or give details when unsure; check who you are dealing with; act quickly if something feels wrong.

misconceptions: Scams are obvious. Scammers use professional websites, fake news, celebrity endorsements and AI-made content.
Only the gullible lose money. The report says education, wealth and age give no immunity.
Early small payouts prove the platform is real. They are part of the script.
The most-reported contact method is the most costly. Email had the most reports and only 5.0% of those reporters lost money.
A guaranteed return is a selling point. Legitimate investments always carry some risk.
sequence: The scale (NASC 2025): $2.18 billion reported, $837.7 million in investment scams.
The pattern of an AI-assisted investment scam, in order.
Red flags and the check (AFS licence, AFCA directory, ASIC prospectus).
Payment red flags and the data: cryptocurrency and digital currency exchanges $121.3 million, bank transfers $118.1 million.
Reports against losses: email 84,861 reports with 4,329 (5.0%) losing money; phone 2,012 reports with loss and a median loss of $3,800.
Who loses: anyone; older Australians are 17.1% of the population and 26.5% of Scamwatch losses.
The super version: illegal early-access schemes (link to lesson 8).
examples: From the report: investment scams are the largest category of combined loss, $837.7 million, down 11.4% from $945.0 million in 2024.
Invented offers for sorting, labelled so.

figures.learnerAction: Read which category is largest and which grew.

figures.learnerAction: Read which method dominates.
